# CEPL: On-site generation for AI-driven grid capex

## Bear case first
The filings describe the AI data center theme [4] and a reference design [13], but no design wins, no named data center order, and no quantified market size. Revenue is concentrated in two customers [2], and the only dated event is a CARB Notice of Violation [3]. Insider buying is small (Form 4), and the customer graph is thin: no federal awards and two named entities (USASpending; customer graph).

## Business today
Capstone sells distributed power generation and microgrid systems, including CHP, ICHP, CCHP, and inverter-based island-capable equipment [0][1], for data center, station power, port, and critical power applications [5]. Reported revenue was $106.004MM and cash was $28.179MM as of 2026-03-31 (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
Order-2 beneficiary in the on-site generation and microgrid developer node, mid horizon. Utility interconnection costs and reliability requirements make self-supply economic [6][8]. Its inverter-based technologies are the stabilizing backbone for microgrids [1].

## Customer graph
Named customers are Horizon Power Systems and E-Finity, both enterprise entities [2]; E-Finity is identified as a distributor [14]. Federal awards are $0 (USASpending), and zero other filers name the company (customer graph). Data center end users are unproven.

## Insider and management signal
Form 4 shows net open-market buying of $295M from 6 buys and 0 sales by 6 insiders (Form 4). Management says demand is accelerating due to AI and data centers [4] and that it has begun using its microgrid solutions in an AI/data center reference design [13]. It also discloses AI-infrastructure investments [17], with no quantified targets.

## Street view
Unknown analyst count, consensus n/a, mean target n/a (street view). No firm rating actions are available. Thin coverage is part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
The reference design [13] becomes a standard for AI data center or critical power projects and scales through the two customers [2][14]. Revenue would multiply if the company supplies integrated microgrids and aftermarket services, not just components. That requires slow grid interconnection, volatile demand charges, and no lasting CARB NOV [3] impact. A single design win would be material to the small revenue base, but none is named.

## Evidence
- Distributed generation and energy distribution solutions, including CHP, ICHP, CCHP [0].
- Inverter-based technologies run grid-parallel or island mode and support microgrids with renewables and storage [1].
- Horizon Power Systems and E-Finity were 41% and 12% of quarterly revenue [2].
- CARB issued a Notice of Violation over 27 distributed generation units [3].
- Demand for on-site generation is accelerating, driven by AI infrastructure and data centers [4].
- Offerings cover data centers, station power, and ports [5].
- Grid power is usually less costly than simple-cycle distributed generation, but utilities may impose interconnection costs and fees [6].
- On-site generation helps when interconnection is costly, reliability is critical, or peak shaving is advantageous [8].
- The company has begun using its microgrid solutions in an AI and data center reference design package [13].
- E-Finity is one of the company's distributors [14].
- It has made investments and may continue to make partnerships related to AI-infrastructure and data centers [17].

## Sizing and survivability
At $3.379MM average daily volume, about 10 trading days to build a position (reality check). Net cash of $2.859MM and 44.6 quarters of runway cover near-term needs (reality check). Share count up 1.1% with shelf on file means dilution is a watch item, not an immediate threat.

## What would change our mind
A named data center customer would appear in a 10-Q or 10-K and would validate the reference design [13]. A Form 4 showing insider sales or no follow-through buying would weaken the signal. A federal award would appear in USASpending and broaden the customer graph.

# XIFR: A renewable developer monetizing interconnection scarcity as data center load crowds the queue

## Bear case first
The short thesis fails if XIFR is worth more as a liquidator than a developer. The July formation of the Mammoth Plains and Carousel JVs and the completed interconnection asset sales [0] show queue position converts into cash before the backlog binds. Guidance assumes the CEPF 3 sale and NextEra transactions close [1]; data center-driven demand [4] may support power prices for the existing fleet. The filings do not quantify these proceeds, so the short cannot prove the sales are distressed rather than opportunistic. Insider activity is neutral at $0 net (Form 4), and customer evidence is thin, which is common for wholesale PPAs but still unproven.

## Business today
XIFR owns wholesale wind and solar generation in a capital-intensive, commodity business [9], selling power under PPAs and selling interconnection assets and rights to co-investors such as NextEra [0]. Revenue was $197MM as of 2017-12-31; current cash was not disclosed (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
XIFR occupies the renewable project developer node, order 2, at-risk, long horizon. Data center load consumes interconnection studies, transmission upgrades, and EPC capacity, delaying renewable projects and raising construction costs. XIFR sidesteps that mechanism by selling interconnection rights rather than building behind them [0].

## Customer graph
No federal awards (USASpending); no named customers in the excerpts; one other filer names XIFR. NextEra is the only enterprise counterparty visible, as co-investor and purchaser of interconnection assets [0], but amounts are undisclosed. All other buyers are unproven.

## Insider and management signal
Form 4 shows zero insider open-market trades: 0 buys, 0 sales, net $0 (Form 4). Management is specific, naming JVs, July closings, repowering and battery storage [0][8], with guidance conditioned on the CEPF 3 sale and NextEra transactions [1].

## Street view
Sell-side coverage is unknown: analyst count, consensus, and mean target are n/a (Street view). Thin coverage removes downgrade risk but also removes institutional validation.

## Non-linear case
The downside compounds if data center load consumes the remaining interconnection capacity. The CEPF 3 sale and NextEra transactions [1] close below assumptions or fail, and the shelf is drawn. The wind permitting pause and FERC interconnection rule changes [7] push repowering [8] past viability, while third-party transmission constraints [2] strand existing output. Each distressed sale validates a lower NAV; with only a 2017 revenue baseline (SEC XBRL), the market re-rates XIFR to liquidation value below the $748MM cap.

## Evidence
- [0] 8-K (2026-07-28): XIFR formed the Mammoth Plains and Carousel battery storage JVs with NextEra and completed associated sales of interconnection assets and rights in July.
- [1] 8-K (2026-07-28): Guidance assumes completion of the CEPF 3 sale and the NextEra co-investment transactions.
- [2] 8-K (2026-07-28): XIFR relies on third-party interconnection and transmission; insurance does not cover all significant losses.
- [4] 10-K (2026-02-17): U.S. power demand expected to grow from data centers, onshoring, and electrification, raising clean energy demand.
- [7] 10-K (2026-02-17): 2025 regulatory actions include a federal executive order pausing wind permitting and FERC approval of interconnection rule proposals.
- [8] 10-K (2026-02-17): XIFR intends to use retained cash for repowering and co-located battery storage.
- [9] 10-K (2026-02-17): Wholesale power generation is capital-intensive and commodity-driven.

## Sizing and survivability
Average daily dollar volume is $11.2MM, about 3 trading days to build a position (Reality check). Net cash is unknown, a shelf is on file, and dilution risk is real if anticipated transactions [1] do not fund repowering [8]. Liquidity works for a small fund, but the unknown runway makes this an event-driven short.

## What would change our mind
1. A Form 4 with insider open-market buying.
2. An 8-K disclosing a named data center or utility interconnection or PPA transaction with dollar amounts.
3. A 10-K with current revenue and proceeds from interconnection sales, proving materiality against the $748MM market cap.

# DUOT: Gas turbine wind-down leaves the grid capex supercycle without a vehicle

## Bear case first
The disconfirming reading is that DUOT's gas turbine business is ending, not accelerating. Duos Energy exists only to wind down the Asset Management Agreement [1], and the company is redeploying capital toward data center infrastructure [14]. The 850 MW Fortress program has no disclosed milestones or follow-on work [7]. The named customers are concentrated in one transaction: Fortress, New APR, and Sawgrass all appear in the same December 2024 contract series [15][16]. No insider buying provides conviction (Form 4).

## Business today
The company sells modular edge data centers, hosting and colocation services, and procurement, logistics, and deployment support for data center projects [2][9]. Revenue was $27.0MM and cash was $1.9MM (SEC XBRL). Duos Energy supports the wind-down of the Asset Management Agreement [1].

## Chain position
DUOT occupies the gas turbine and power generation equipment node, but as a service operator under a wind-down agreement, not as an order beneficiary. The theme's logic is that data center load drives gas turbine orders and aftermarket service. DUOT's service revenue is tied to 30 mobile gas turbines being wound down [1][7].

## Customer graph
Fortress Investment Group, New APR, and Sawgrass APR Holdings LLC are enterprise buyers named in filings [7][15][16]. The Department of Transportation is a government buyer with a $2.6MM federal award (USASpending). One other filer names the company (USASpending). Customer evidence is concentrated in a single Fortress-related transaction.

## Insider and management signal
Open-market insider activity was net $0 across 0 buys and 0 sales by 0 insiders over the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Management provides specific details on the Fortress agreement and the 30 mobile gas turbine generators [7], but the emphasis is on wind-down and redeployment to data centers [14].

## Street view
No sell-side coverage exists. Analyst count is unknown, consensus is n/a, and mean target is n/a. Thin coverage is itself part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
The path to a multiple requires the Fortress relationship to expand beyond wind-down into new gas turbine service contracts, or the 850 MW fleet to generate recurring service revenue for DUOT [7]. The filings do not show a pipeline for new AMA-style contracts. Without that, the theme and the business remain disconnected.

## Evidence
- Continuing operations are conducted through Duos Edge AI and Duos Technology Solutions, with Duos Energy supporting the wind-down of the Asset Management Agreement [1]
- Principal business activities include edge data center infrastructure, hosting and colocation, and technology solutions for data center projects [2]
- Duos engaged with Fortress to assist in the purchase of approximately 850 MW of generation capacity consisting of 30 mobile gas turbine generators [7]
- Duos Edge develops modular edge data centers for AI workloads and latency-sensitive applications [9]
- The divestiture represents the company's complete exit from rail technology and redeployment toward data center infrastructure [14]
- In December 2024, the company entered contracts with Fortress to deploy and operate a fleet of mobile gas turbines and balance-of-plant inventory, providing management, sales and operations functions to Sawgrass [15][16]

## Sizing and survivability
A small fund can build a position in about 4 trading days at $10.5MM average daily dollar volume (reality check). Net cash is $1.9MM and cash runway is about 0.6 quarters (reality check). Share count is up 62.1% in 12 months (reality check). A shelf registration is on file (reality check). The cash constraint and dilution risk threaten the thesis.

## What would change our mind
- A new or expanded gas turbine service contract with Fortress or another counterparty, disclosed in an 8-K or 10-Q with named capacity and start date.
- Form 4 open-market insider buying of DUOT common stock.
- A federal award or new named customer contract for gas turbine-related services that extends the cash runway beyond 4 quarters.

# SLNH: Data center load growth creates an ERCOT demand response option, not a software compounder

## Bear case first
The software thesis fails. The filings define Grid Demand Response Services as services that support generating and delivering electricity, not as a software product [4], and demand response revenue is a reconciling item outside the four reportable segments [14]. Q2 2025 demand response revenue was $161M on total revenue of $6.158MM [18]. Insider net open-market selling was -$649.219M over the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Customer evidence is thin: federal awards total $14.45M from two agencies (USASpending), and no named enterprise customer appears in the provided excerpts.

## Business today
The company operates data centers co-located with wind, solar, and hydroelectric generation [6] and earns revenue from cryptocurrency mining, data center hosting, high-performance computing, and demand response services [15][16]. H1 2025 total revenue was $12.094MM, including $668M of demand response revenue [19]; fiscal 2025 revenue was $29.717MM and cash was $0.462MM (SEC XBRL). Data center hosting revenue comes from third-party Bitcoin mining customers at Project Sophie, Dorothy, and Kati [12], and the company owns Briscoe Wind Farm, whose electricity is delivered to the Dorothy data centers [17].

## Chain position
SLNH occupies the grid services node below the software layer: it uses its data centers to deliver demand response to grid operators [15] and can generate demand response revenue from any data center activity [16]. The economic logic is that on-site load and generation create dispatchable capacity, but the filing describes services, not software, and demand response is not a reportable segment [14]. The company is a beneficiary of the capex cycle through services contracts, not a software platform with recurring license revenue.

## Customer graph
The identifiable paying parties are government agencies: $10.69M from the Department of Veterans Affairs and $3.76M from the Department of Defense, for total federal awards of $14.45M (USASpending). Data center hosting customers are third-party Bitcoin miners, but no named enterprise customer is disclosed in the provided excerpts [12]. These government awards are immaterial relative to revenue, and one other SEC filer names the company (Dossier).

## Insider and management signal
Insider conviction is negative on open-market activity: net -$649.219M across 3 buys and 30 sales in the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Management language is detailed and forward-looking: the strategy is co-located data centers supporting compute-intensive applications [6], and any data center activity can produce demand response revenue [16]. The filings also describe an ERCOT power trading or demand response program with a partner, with the achievement date to be mutually agreed [11].

## Street view
No sell-side coverage is reported: analyst count is n/a, consensus is n/a, and mean target is n/a (Street view). Paywalled bank reports are not identified. For an under-covered small cap, thin coverage is part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
The non-linear path starts with the ERCOT program: once SLC and the company agree on power trading or demand response parameters, the distribution waterfall changes and class B members receive 92.5% of distributable cash after an 18% IRR target [11]. ERCOT spans more than 46,500 miles of transmission and 680 generation units [1], so a small share of that market would be a multiple of the current $668M first-half demand response revenue [19]. The HPC/AI segment is a second upside leg: the company may lease HPC assets or HPC/AI data centers to third parties [13], and GPU-as-a-service is sold per GPU-hour [3]. For this outcome, the company must survive its cash position and reach the ERCOT achievement date.

## Evidence
- [1] ERCOT connects more than 46,500 miles of transmission lines and over 680 generation units.
- [3] GPU-as-a-service is the sale or lease of GPU clusters, typically per GPU-hour.
- [4] Grid Demand Response Services are services provided to support generating and delivering electricity to the grid.
- [6] The company strategy is to operate data centers co-located with wind, solar, and hydroelectric plants.
- [11] ERCOT Achievement Date is the date SLC and the company agree on power trading or demand response parameters; after it, class A members receive 7.5% and class B members 92.5% of distributable cash until the 18% IRR target return date.
- [12] Data Center Hosting segment revenue comes from third-party Bitcoin mining customers at Project Sophie, Dorothy, and Kati.
- [13] HPC services may generate revenue from sale or lease of HPC assets or HPC/AI data centers.
- [14] Demand response revenue is a reconciling item and is not included in the four reportable segments.
- [15] The company uses its data centers to deliver demand response services to grid operators or utilities.
- [16] Any service at the data centers, including mining, hosting, or AI, can generate demand response revenue.
- [17] Intersegment eliminations reflect Briscoe wind farm electricity delivered to Dorothy data centers.
- [18] Q2 2025 segment revenue from external customers was $5.997MM; demand response revenue was $161M, for $6.158MM total consolidated revenue.
- [19] H1 2025 segment revenue from external customers was $11.426MM; demand response revenue was $668M, for $12.094MM total consolidated revenue.

## Sizing and survivability
A small fund can build a position in about 2 trading days based on average daily dollar volume of $22.177MM (Reality check). Net cash is -$17.437MM and cash runway is about 0.2 quarters (Reality check); share count rose 711.4% in 12 months and a shelf registration is on file (Reality check). These facts threaten the thesis and require equity or debt financing before the ERCOT path can play out.

## What would change our mind
- A Form 4 filing showing sustained open-market insider buying, not selling, would counter the current insider signal.
- A 10-Q or 8-K announcing the ERCOT Achievement Date or a named demand response contract would tie the opportunity to a revenue event.
- A federal award or named customer disclosure of material size in a 10-Q or USASpending would fix the missing customer validation.

# T1 Energy: Avoid solar module supplier with unverified backlog and delay risk.

## Bear case first
T1's stated 5.4 GW of customer contracts [7] is not a firm revenue commitment; contracts can be amended to decrease volume or change delivery schedules [9]. The provided filing excerpts do not name any customer, and federal award data shows no government demand (USASpending). Insider open-market sales totaled $1.9MM against no buys (Form 4). Production is concentrated in a single facility [5], and inventory rose from $116.0MM to $228.8MM in six months [10]. A renewable project delay cycle would push module deliveries later, compress pricing, and expose this concentration.

## Business today
T1 manufactures and sells PV solar modules in the United States, with one operating segment [1][11]. Modules are produced at G1_Dallas, which became fully operational in Q2 2025 [17]. 2025 revenue was $755.295MM and cash was $182.450MM (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
T1 sits at the equipment supplier node of the US grid capex adoption chain. The data center load story creates module demand, but suppliers face order pushouts and pricing pressure when renewable projects slip. For an at-risk node, the company is a short or avoid candidate, not a long.

## Customer graph
The provided filing excerpts report customer contracts for 5.4 GW [7] but do not identify the buyers. Federal awards are $0 (USASpending), and no other filer names the company (customer graph). Enterprise customers are unproven; government customers are absent.

## Insider and management signal
Trailing 12-month Form 4 activity is net selling of $1,871,777 across four open-market sales and zero buys (Form 4). Management gives quantified delivery schedules [8], a 5.4 GW contracted volume [7], and a Q1 2027 cell production start [3]. The operational specificity does not offset the absence of insider buying.

## Street view
Sell-side coverage is absent: analyst count unknown, consensus n/a, mean target n/a (Street view). No firm rating actions are visible. The stock is under-covered, which removes a support channel when the bear thesis is active.

## Non-linear case
The downside scenario is a delay-oversupply spiral. Customers use amendment rights [9] to push 2026 and 2027 deliveries [8] into later years or cancel. T1 remains at a single facility [5] with rising finished goods inventory [10]. Net cash is -$207.708MM and share count is up 88.9 percent with a shelf on file (Reality check), so an equity raise is a likely part of the path. The result is a share price far below today's level.

## Evidence
- T1 manufactures and sells PV solar modules in the United States [1].
- A facility is anticipated to begin production of TOPCon solar cells in Q1 2027 [3].
- PV solar modules are currently produced at a single facility in the United States [5].
- Contracts with customers for future sale of 5.4 GW of PV solar modules exist as of June 30, 2026 [7].
- T1 expects to recognize sales of 1.5 GW in the remainder of 2026, 1.3 GW in 2027, and 2.6 GW thereafter through 2029 [8].
- These contracts may be amended to increase or decrease volume or change delivery schedules [9].
- Inventory at June 30, 2026 was $228.773MM total, including $225.562MM of raw materials and $2.024MM of finished goods, versus $116.043MM total at December 31, 2025 [10].
- The single operating segment derives revenue from the manufacturing and sale of PV solar modules [11].
- G1_Dallas became fully operational in Q2 2025 and production increased through 2025 [17].

## Sizing and survivability
Average daily dollar volume is $280.874MM, so a small fund can build a position in about one trading day (Reality check). Net cash is -$207.708MM, share count rose 88.9 percent in 12 months, and a shelf registration is on file (Reality check). The liquidity is adequate, but the negative cash position, dilution history, and shelf do not support a long thesis.

## What would change our mind
A 10-Q or 10-K naming a contracted customer would improve the unproven customer evidence. A Form 4 showing an insider open-market buy would change the insider signal. A USASpending federal award to T1 would add a government buyer.

# WS: US grid capex supercycle driven by data center load, 2026-2030

## Bear case first

Why this name fails. Electrical steel laminations may be a small product line inside a $3,443.8MM revenue base (SEC XBRL); the filings give no revenue breakdown. The customer graph shows no named customers and $0 federal awards, so customer validation is unproven (customer graph, USASpending). The 10-K calls the industry fragmented and competitive [4] and warns that electrical steel supply could be curtailed [11]. With no open-market insider buying, the insider signal is neutral (Form 4).

## Business today

Worthington Steel is a value-added processor of carbon flat-rolled steel and a producer of electrical steel laminations [0][2]. Its processing includes slitting and cutting-to-length [1]. Revenue was $3,443.8MM and cash was $84.6MM (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position

The chain position is electrical steel processing and slitting services, an order 3 beneficiary with a mid horizon. Data center load drives grid capex, transformer production, then electrical steel processing. In toll processing, the customer keeps title to steel [3], so the processor earns conversion fees rather than steel price risk; fee pricing power is not disclosed.

## Customer graph

Named enterprise customers: none, so enterprise buyers are unproven (customer graph). Government: $0 federal awards, so government demand is unproven (USASpending). One other filer names Worthington Steel, but the relationship is not described (customer graph). The 10-K lists end markets [19] but names no specific customer.

## Insider and management signal

Form 4 shows net open-market insider activity of $0 across 0 buys and 0 sales (Form 4). That is no conviction signal. Management cites data center demand as a possible electricity driver [12] and says capacity projects support electrical steel growth [13], but gives no quantified targets.

## Street view

Sell-side aggregators show unknown analysts, consensus n/a, and mean target n/a (Street view). No firm rating actions are visible. Thin coverage is part of the setup.

## Non-linear case

A sustained data center load cycle could force transformer OEMs to add electrical steel lamination capacity. Worthington Steel already makes precision magnetic steel laminations for transformer and motor industries [2]. If conversion fees rise and electrical steel becomes a larger share of revenue, the business mix could change. The path requires named customers, multi-year contracts, and capacity projects [13] converting into volume. Without a revenue breakdown, optionality is unproven.

## Evidence

- Value-added processor of carbon flat-rolled steel and producer of electrical steel laminations [0][2].
- Processing includes slitting and cutting-to-length [1].
- Electrical steel laminations serve automotive, industrial motor, generator, and transformer industries [2].
- Toll processing: customer retains title to the steel [3].
- Steel processing industry is fragmented and highly competitive [4].
- Supply curtailment of flat-rolled steel or electrical steel could harm results [11].
- Data center electricity demand could contribute to infrastructure costs or power constraints [12].
- Capacity projects support growth in markets such as electrical steel [13].
- End markets include automotive, heavy truck, agriculture, construction, and energy [19].

## Sizing and survivability

A small fund can own this name: average daily dollar volume is $10.6MM, so building a position takes about 4 trading days (Reality check). Cash is $84.6MM and net cash is $13.2MM; cash runway cannot be calculated (SEC XBRL, Reality check). Share count rose 0.4 percent in 12 months, so dilution is not a current threat (Reality check). Shelf status is not stated in the reality check facts.

## What would change our mind

A 10-Q or 10-K that discloses electrical steel laminations revenue or segment profit and shows it as material would strengthen the thesis. A Form 4 with open-market insider buying would add a conviction signal. A federal award to Worthington Steel in USASpending, or a named transformer OEM customer in a filing, would validate the customer graph.

# ESP: A high-voltage equipment maker tied to the grid capex cycle, with thin filings and heavy insider selling

## Bear case first
The strongest bear reading is that ESP is a small supplier with no disclosed grid-specific strategy and no named customers. The filing lists products but no backlog, pricing, or capacity data, so the grid capex thesis cannot be confirmed from the 10-Q. Insider selling is heavy: 134 open-market sales and no buys in the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Federal awards are concentrated in DoD rather than commercial utility or data center orders (USASpending). The company could be a fringe supplier while the high-voltage equipment cycle flows to larger manufacturers.

## Business today
ESP's primary products are power supplies, power converters, filters, power transformers, magnetic components, power distribution equipment, UPS systems, and antennas [0]. As of 2025-06-30, revenue was $9.6MM and cash was $18.9MM (SEC XBRL). The shown payer is federal, primarily DoD (USASpending), and no named enterprise customers appear in the excerpt [0].

## Chain position
ESP occupies the high-voltage equipment manufacturing node, an order-1 beneficiary of grid capex. The relevant products in the filing are power transformers and power distribution equipment [0]. If utilities and data center developers extend lead times and pay higher prices, the cycle translates into revenue growth and margin expansion for this node.

## Customer graph
Government: USASpending shows federal awards to ESP of $18.7MM, all from the Department of Defense. Enterprise: unproven, because the excerpt names no utility, data center, or commercial customer [0]. One other SEC filer names ESP (customer graph), but no named customers are present. Commercial demand evidence is thin.

## Insider and management signal
Trailing 12-month Form 4 data show 0 open-market buys and 134 open-market sales, net -$1.7MM (Form 4). Management language in the filing is limited to a product list; there are no strategic commitments, capacity additions, or grid-related targets [0]. The insider signal is negative.

## Street view
Sell-side aggregators list no firm-rated analysts, no consensus, and no mean target (sell-side aggregators). No recent rating actions are reported. This is an under-covered small cap, and thin coverage is part of the potential setup.

## Non-linear case
The non-linear path is that a small number of utility or DoD orders fills existing capacity, pushing operating margin above its current cost base. The $9.6MM revenue base (SEC XBRL) means a single large contract can be material. Operating leverage is the mechanism: prices rise, fixed costs stay flat, and incremental revenue drops through to operating income. This path requires ESP to be qualified as a supplier, which the filing does not show. The filing also discloses no new segment investment, so the path rests on existing products [0].

## Evidence
- The 10-Q filed 2026-05-12 lists ESP's primary products as power supplies, power converters, filters, power transformers, magnetic components, power distribution equipment, UPS systems, and antennas [0].

## Sizing and survivability
Average daily dollar volume is $2.9MM, so a $189MM position can be built in roughly 12 trading days (delayed price data, SEC XBRL). Net cash is $18.9MM against $9.6MM revenue (SEC XBRL). Share count rose 7.1% in 12 months (SEC XBRL), a real dilution risk for the thesis.

## What would change our mind
1. A 10-Q or 10-K discloses a named utility customer or grid-related backlog. 2. Form 4 shows an open-market insider buy, reversing the 0-buy/134-sale pattern. 3. USASpending shows a new federal award to ESP for power transformers or power distribution equipment.

# SMXT: Grid capex supercycle exposure is contractual, not a new testing franchise

## Bear case first
The 8-K's testing and commissioning clauses are obligations inside a single BESS EPC contract, not a standalone business line [12]. The thesis requires SMXT to sit at the testing/commissioning node, but the filing shows contractor testing, not third-party certification sold to utilities [16]. There are no insider buys, no named customers, no federal awards, and the share count rose 24.2 percent in 12 months (Form 4, USASpending, reality check). The filing does not quantify testing revenue or show a second project, leaving the revenue base behind the thesis an open question.

## Business today
SMXT acts as contractor under a utility-scale BESS agreement filed with its 8-K [0]. It procures, constructs, installs and tests the battery and all interconnection facilities required to connect to the local utility's transmission system [12]. Revenue was $90.98MM and cash was $7.97MM at 2025-12-31 (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
Testing and commissioning are contract deliverables inside the EPC scope; the contractor cannot energize the battery without the owner's written approval [7]. The owner holds the interconnection agreement [13][19]. SMXT sits at the EPC node, not the independent certification node, so the thesis's economic logic does not match the evidence.

## Customer graph
The buyer is unproven: the only counterparty is the "Owner" of the BESS project, not named in the excerpts [0]. No enterprise customer is named, federal awards are $0, and no other filer names SMXT (USASpending). Customer evidence is thin and unproven.

## Insider and management signal
No insider bought or sold stock in the trailing 12 months, a net $0 read on conviction (Form 4). Management language is contractually firm: $5M per day liquidated damages for missed mechanical completion, full risk for interconnection cost, and clear acceptance testing criteria [17][9][3].

## Street view
No sell-side coverage exists; analyst count is unknown, consensus is n/a, and mean target is n/a (Street view). For an under-covered $197MM small-cap, thin coverage is itself part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
For the thesis to pay a multiple, SMXT would need to convert this EPC execution into a repeatable testing/commissioning franchise with utilities as named customers. That path requires evidence outside this filing: follow-on awards, a separate testing/commissioning segment, or disclosed backlog. Any pipeline beyond this project is an open question.

## Evidence
